questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
questions.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -7\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}$ and $C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -3 \\ -4 & 6 & -7 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 7 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 & -10\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
questions.problem:
Let $B={{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & a \\ b & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & c & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=0,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-5.$

questions.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
questions.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 9 \\ -3 & -7\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
questions.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 9 \\ -3 & -7\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-7)-9\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}-7 & -9 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
questions.problem: Let $B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 11\end{aligned}]}$  be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 11 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}11 & -2 \\ -5 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
questions.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
questions.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\cdot 4-2\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -\frac{3}{2} & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
